newsitem.title: UK: BOE softens tone on rates in inflation report.
newsitem.headline: BOE softens tone on rates in inflation report.

text.p: The Bank of England has clearly softened its tone on the need for tighter UK monetary policy, and been forced to take on board the pound's extended rally and signs of slowing domestic demand, analysts said on Wednesday.
"This is a far throw from the half point rise called for in the December minutes and tallies with the softer tone in Howard Davies' speech on Tuesday," said Alex Garrard, UBS' economist.
"And the quarter point rise Davies called for yesterday has been translated into the need for a moderate rise with maybe a further rise later in the year in the inflation report."

The Bank in its quarterly inflation report it continued to see the need for a moderate tightening of monetary policy to ensure the government's 2.5 percent inflation target can be met two years ahead.

"The Bank's central projection for inflation two years ahead is close to three percent and rising...In the light of the central projection and the risks surrounding it, the Bank continues to see the need for a moderate tightening of policy."
The report did not specify how big a rate increase the Bank would like to see.
But deputy governor Howard Davies said on Tuesday the Bank favoured an early quarter-point rise from the present 6.0 percent, perhaps followed by another rise later this year.
Garrard said the Bank's change of emphasis owes much to the continued strength of sterling and signs domestic demand is easing slightly.
"Sterling has extended way beyond the Bank's presumption that it would be temporary and not really matter, and the domestic sector looks like it is slowing of its own accord."
Analysts said the Bank may be playing a tactical game and laying the ground for a rate rise after the general election, which must be held by May.

"It may be tactical -- a recognition that it has not won the argument and its advice was not taken. And the Bank doesn't want pick too much of a fight with Clarke," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.
Dicks said the Bank now knows it cannot get its way on rates before the election so, "it is setting the stage for afterwards".
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke agreed Bank of England Governor Eddie George had toned down his advice on monetary policy since the December 11 monetary meeting.
"The Governor has actually slightly modified and toned down his advice since the December meeting," he told ITN.
At the December 11 monetary meeting, George said if rates did not rise immediately by a quarter point, it was likely they would need to rise by a half point in January or February.
But Dicks said while the Bank may have toned down its advice on monetary policy, it has hardened its line on the risk of higher inflation in the future.

In recent inflation reports, the Bank talked about the change in the risks surrounding the forecast, Dicks said. "This time it has emphasised its two-year projection for inflation is three percent and rising. That is quite a forceful line."
